 Texas launches first statewide audit of election results
 Published 7:00 pm Thursday, November 19, 2026
 By Jakob Gurley

 AUSTIN — Texas is conducting its first statewide risk-limiting audit following the Nov. 3 general election, implementing a law authored by state Sen. Lois Kolkhorst, R-Brenham, to strengthen election security and verify the accuracy of reported results. 
 The Texas Secretary of State’s Office announced two separate post-election audit procedures designed to compare electronically tabulated results with paper ballots. 
 The statewide risk-limiting audit, required under Senate Bill 598, uses statistical sampling and randomly selected paper ballots to independently verify the reported outcome of a statewide race or proposition. 
 Kolkhorst, who authored the legislation during the 2021 legislative session, represents Senate District 18, which includes Victoria, DeWitt, Goliad, Calhoun, Lavaca, Refugio and Aransas counties. 
 The law applies to elections held after Aug. 31, 2026, that include a statewide contest or measure and use an auditable voting system. The Nov. 3 general election marks the first statewide election subject to the requirement. 
 For this election, the U.S. Senate race was selected for the risk-limiting audit.

 Secretary of State Robert S. Howden was scheduled to generate a 10-digit random number Wednesday to determine which paper ballots would be examined. 
 The selection process was scheduled to be livestreamed, with the audit set to begin Thursday, Nov. 19, and continue until completed. 
 Unlike traditional recounts, which may involve examining every ballot in a race, risk-limiting audits use statistical methods to select a sample of ballots and assess whether the reported outcome is accurate. 
 The process provides an independent check of electronic voting results using voter-verifiable paper records. 
 Senate Bill 598 also established requirements for auditable voting systems, including the production of paper records that voters can verify. 
 Under the law, those systems cannot connect to the internet or another computer network. 
 Beginning Sept. 1, 2026, direct-recording electronic voting machines without a voter-verifiable paper audit trail could no longer be used, except under certain circumstances involving curbside voting. 
 The legislation also established a pilot program in 2022, allowing the Secretary of State’s Office to test risk-limiting audit procedures in selected counties before statewide implementation. 
 Separate hand counts also required 
 In addition to the statewide risk-limiting audit, Texas counties must conduct post-election hand counts under requirements amended by Senate Bill 1, authored by state Sen. Bryan Hughes during the 2021 legislative session. 
 The hand-count process requires election officials to manually examine ballots from randomly selected polling locations and precincts, comparing the results with electronic vote totals to identify discrepancies. 
 For the Nov. 3 election, the Secretary of State’s Office selected two statewide contests for the hand count: the U.S. Senate race and the chief justice of the Texas Supreme Court race. 
 Each county’s general custodian of election records must also select a third contested race for examination. 
 Counties are required to manually count ballots from at least three Election Day polling locations and three early voting locations, or 1% of those locations, whichever is greater. 
 Mail-in ballots must also be counted from at least three precincts, or 1% of precincts in which mail ballots were cast, whichever is greater. 
 Although both procedures involve examining paper ballots, they serve different purposes. 
 The risk-limiting audit uses statistical sampling to assess the accuracy of the reported outcome in a selected statewide contest. The post-election hand count compares manually counted ballot samples with electronic totals across selected polling locations and races. 
 Together, the procedures provide additional checks on election results and voting equipment. 
 The Secretary of State’s Office said implementing statewide risk-limiting audits adds another layer of accountability and transparency to Texas elections. 
 Jakob Gurley is a multimedia journalist with the Victoria Advocate. He can be reached at jakob.gurley@vicad.com.
